resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1821 stone tower and the 1881 cast-iron tower are both on the site. Sources that give 1881 describe the present tower; the form and the USLHS record date the first light to 1821.

The MHC chronology gives the 1821 stone tower and the 1881 cast-iron replacement; LighthouseFriends gives 1881 for the cast-iron tower and its dwelling. Both are consistent once the two towers are separated.

notes_for_editor: Matched by identity: the roster is the USLHS record (roster.py --json), keepers in order. Unresolved: (1) Lens: the USLHS record and the form's chronology imply a fifth-order original optic; LighthouseFriends says a sixth-order lens came in 1856 and the fifth-order lens was in place until 1956. The form's 1925 entries name both fourth and fifth orders. Not settled here. (2) Status: the station record says active; the USLHS place record and LighthouseFriends describe a station discontinued in 1956 and relit in 1989. No source read says whether the lamp burns today. (3) Relighting date: 7 August 1989 (LighthouseFriends) against 5 August (marker). (4) Oil house: the form dates its granite walls to 1821; LighthouseFriends says an oil house was added in 1906. (5) The 1889 characteristic change comes from LighthouseFriends only; the form's 1919 flash entry is letter-spaced in the OCR and was not used. (6) The MHC form's coordinates (40 36'7"N) are a typo for 42 degrees; the station record's coordinates are right. (7) The 1842 inspector's report and the 1820 Congressional allocation are quoted by LighthouseFriends only; the originals were not read. (8) The 1880 Homer stay is confirmed by the Philadelphia Museum of Art; the 'about fifty views' figure is LighthouseFriends' own. (9) LighthouseFriends calls Edward H. Hopkins the last keeper; the USLHS roster lists Andrew M. McLaughlin for 1955-1956. (10) The hatchery (1889-1954), the 1906 oil house and the 1940 Flying Santa story rest on LighthouseFriends alone. The Christmas story's keeper is named; the keeper's son is not. (11) The Lighthouse Service Bulletin does not mention this station in the corpus. The Life-Saving Service stranding tables list 'Ten Pound Island' but are OCR tables; no column reading was used, so the Storms chapter is left out. (12) Newspaper search (Chronicling America, 1820-1935, MA) returned three Massachusetts pages (1869, 1877, 1909) that were not read: the rate limit timed out, and they look unrelated. (13) The lens order, the 1856 change and the 1889 characteristic should be checked against the Lighthouse Board annual reports, which this corpus does not cover before 1891. (18) The 1919 flash entry (form p. 4 of 6: 'fixed light with flash 6 seconds- 5 seconds') was read from the form's text and checked on the page image; the 1889 date stays LighthouseFriends' only. The story states the two dates as unsettled. (19) The Philadelphia Museum record does not name the keeper; Merrill is named by LighthouseFriends (roster 1865-1883). (20) USLHS lists the Coast Guard as Owner/Manager and 'Open to Public: No'; the 1981 form and LighthouseFriends say the City of Gloucester owns the island and light, with a 0.1-acre Coast Guard parcel. The story states both. (21) The 1894 Light-House Board entry (Tenpound Island, item 76) is in the report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1894; the story uses that year.
